item.title: Safety Verification for Voltage Control in Inverter Dominated Radial Distribution Networks under Actuator and Sensor Adversarial Attacks
item.description: arXiv:2610.41910v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper develops a safety verification framework for inverter-based radial distribution networks under sensor and actuator attacks. Each customer is equipped with a droop-based controller to regulate its voltage within a desirable bound of a reference, i.e., to achieve safety. In our setting, attacks and disturbances enter the droop-based controllers, while actuator attacks corrupt the reactive power injected into the network. Consequently, invariance of the controller state alone does not guarantee compliance with inverter capacities or customer voltage limits. To address this challenge, we derive conditions to guarantee that the reactive power state remains inside a predefined ellipsoid, while at the same time ensuring that the attacked reactive power injections and customer voltages respect predetermined operating limits that hold uniformly for the entire predefined ellipsoid. Together, these conditions guarantee safety under all admissible disturbances and state-dependent sensor and actuator attacks. Finally, we express the resulting containment condition as a linear matrix inequality (LMI) feasibility problem. A five-customer radial network based on the CIGRE benchmark corroborates our theoretical developments in simulations.
item.dc:creator: Georgios Pantazis, Revi Boelen, Michelle S. Chong

item.title: The Quartic Gap Between Quantum and Dequantized Algorithms for Linear Algebra Is Tight
item.description: arXiv:2610.42069v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantum algorithms for linear algebra that access a matrix $A$ through quantum random access memory (QRAM) prepare quantum states proportional to the solutions of linear systems and related problems. Dequantized classical algorithms, when given sampling and query access to $A$, return sampling and query access to an approximate solution. Both kinds of algorithms use a number of queries that is polynomial in the normalized Frobenius norm $\rho=\|A\|_F/\|A\|$ and does not directly depend on the dimension. For linear systems at fixed condition number and accuracy, quantum algorithms use $\widetilde O(\rho)$ queries, whereas the best dequantized algorithms use $\widetilde O(\rho^4)$. We prove that this quartic gap is tight in the worst case, up to a logarithmic factor. For every constant $\kappa_0>1$, we construct dense linear systems with condition number at most $\kappa_0$ for which sampling from the solution within a sufficiently small constant total variation distance requires $\Omega(\rho^4/\log\rho)$ classical queries but only $\Theta(\rho)$ quantum queries. The same separation holds, for errors below smaller thresholds, for positive-definite systems, least squares, ridge regression, matrix powers and square roots, imaginary-time and real-time Hamiltonian evolution, and sampling from the top principal component. Our results therefore show that many quantum algorithms for linear algebra, achieve a near-quartic speedup in the worst case, over classical algorithms with sampling and query access. All of these classical lower bounds follow from the same framework, which is based on a lower bound for sampling from distributions that depend on a fixed set of Fourier coefficients of an unknown Boolean function.
item.dc:creator: Shouvanik Chakrabarti, Dylan Herman, Junhyung Lyle Kim, Guneykan Ozgul

item.title: Cost-Aware Stopping for Freeze-Thaw Bayesian Optimization: When Does One-Step Lookahead Suffice?
item.description: arXiv:2610.42085v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Freeze-thaw Bayesian optimization (BO) evaluates candidates in resumable increments but usually stops at a budget or convergence test. We maximize a budget-free utility, the best observed score minus a cost per increment, with a one-step lookahead: advance the candidate with the largest expected improvement (EI) under a fixed surrogate, and stop once no EI exceeds the cost. This rule, EI stopping, never falls below stopping immediately in expected utility, yet it can stop too early. We construct a certificate, a lower bound on the value of two-step lookahead, that proves such a stop premature, and repeating this correction never lowers expected utility under the surrogate. Under the surrogate, EI stops are premature on average at low costs and lose little at high costs. On three hyperparameter optimization benchmarks, a pre-registered test finds EI stopping noninferior to the correction in most high-cost settings, while the correction gains at low costs on two of the three; more information sharing in the surrogate raises EI stopping's utility. On the surrogates of two published methods, EI stopping trades lower scores for fewer training increments. EI stopping is a simple cost-aware reference whose utility depends on the surrogate.
item.dc:creator: Long Vu, Jongseong Brad Choi, Binoy Ravindran, Zhoulai Fu

item.title: Regret-Optimal Wasserstein-Robust Linear Regression
item.description: arXiv:2610.42109v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in terms of their excess risk, or regret. We study this gap for multivariate least-squares regression, assuming that the observed source law and unknown target law differ by an adversarial 2-Wasserstein perturbation of size $\varepsilon$. We first identify the asymptotic complexity of robust decision-making in the $\varepsilon \to 0$ limit, characterized by a problem-specific condition number $\kappa$. Here, a wide spectrum of simple algorithms, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate of $O(\kappa \varepsilon^2)$. For fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, we prove that DRO still achieves the minimax rate if the problem has bounded residual effective rank. On the other hand, we identify significant failure modes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors. Fortunately, we prove that two alternative procedures, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR), attain the minimax rate. We derive an exact convex reformulation of MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR, along with high-probability finite-sample guarantees. We support these theoretical results with numerical experiments separating the performance of MRO and SNR from DRO.
item.dc:creator: Sloan Nietert, Daniel Kuhn

item.title: Learning Maximal Regions of Attraction on Compact Sets using Taylor Lyapunov Networks
item.description: arXiv:2408.17246v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We consider the problem of learning maximal Lyapunov functions to compute the maximal region of attraction of nonlinear dynamical systems using neural networks. Two obstacles limit existing neural-network approaches: 1) finite-width approximations can fail to preserve the strict Lyapunov inequalities near the equilibrium, where they become arbitrarily weak, and 2) training is necessarily performed on a bounded computational domain for which the classical Lyapunov and Zubov theorems do not directly apply. To address these issues, first we derive Lyapunov and Zubov theorems directly on a prescribed compact computational domain, characterizing the maximal region of attraction within that domain as the solution of a boundary-value PDE. Second, we introduce the Taylor Lyapunov network, an architecture that prescribes the quadratic leading-order term via the system's linearization and represents the higher-order remainder through a structured cubic factorization, guaranteeing that any network in this class is a valid local Lyapunov function by construction. Finally, we prove that Taylor Lyapunov networks are universal approximators of maximal Lyapunov functions on compact domains, and combine these results into an unsupervised, physics-informed training procedure. Numerical experiments on systems of varying dimensions and stability types show that the proposed architecture is efficient at estimating the maximum region of attraction.
item.dc:creator: Matthieu Barreau, Nicola Bastianello

item.title: Quadratic obstructions to Small-Time Local Controllability for the multi-input bilinear Schr\"odinger equation
item.description: arXiv:2502.14999v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We investigate the small-time local controllability (STLC) near the ground state of a bilinear Schr\"odinger equation when the linearized system is not controllable. It is well known that, for single-input systems, quadratic terms in the state expansion can then lead to obstructions to the STLC of the nonlinear system. In this work, we extend this phenomenon to the multi-input setting, presenting the first example of multi-input quadratic obstructions for PDEs. Our results build upon our previous study of such obstructions for ODEs and provide a functional framework for analyzing them in the bilinear Schr\"odinger equation.
item.dc:creator: Th\'eo Gherdaoui

item.title: A Riemannian approach for PDE-constrained shape optimization over the diffeomorphism group using outer metrics
item.description: arXiv:2503.22872v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this paper, we study the use of outer metrics, in particular Sobolev-type metrics on the diffeomorphism group in the context of PDE-constrained shape optimization. Leveraging the structure of the diffeomorphism group we analyze the connection between the push-forward of a smooth function defined on the diffeomorphism group and the classical shape derivative as an Eulerian semi-derivative. We consider in particular, two predominant examples on PDE-constrained shape optimization. An electric impedance tomography inspired problem, and the optimization of a two-dimensional bridge. These problems are numerically solved using the Riemannian steepest descent method where the descent directions are taken to be the Riemannian gradients associated to various outer metrics. For comparison reasons, we also solve the problem using other previously proposed Riemannian metrics in particular the Steklov-Poincar\'e metric.
item.dc:creator: Estefania Loayza-Romero, Lidiya Pryymak, Kathrin Welker

item.title: A Markovian Approach for Cross-Category Complementarity in Choice Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2508.18566v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In modern retail and e-commerce, customers often purchase multiple items across distinct product categories, exhibiting both substitution and complementarity. We consider the cross-category assortment optimization problem where retailers jointly determine assortments across categories to maximize expected revenue. Most prior work on the topic either overlooks complementarity or proposes models that lead to intractable optimization problems, despite being based on the multinomial logit (MNL) choice model. We propose a sequential multi-purchase choice model for cross-category choice that incorporates complementarity through a Markovian transition structure across categories, while allowing general Random Utility Maximization (RUM)-based choice models to capture the within-category substitution. We develop an Expectation-Maximization algorithm for estimation, and a polynomial-time algorithm for unconstrained assortment optimization that yields the optimal solution when the within-category substitution follows a Markov chain choice model. Furthermore, we introduce an empirical metric to quantify the strength of complementarity across product categories and conduct extensive numerical experiments using both synthetic data and a large-scale transaction-level dataset from a major U.S. grocery store. Our model improves predictive accuracy and model fit in both synthetic and real-data experiments and improves expected revenue in synthetic settings with complementarity. It also reveals intuitive market structures such as brand-loyal cross-category purchasing. Overall, we believe that our model provides a theoretically grounded and practical framework for modeling complementarity and making better cross-category assortment decisions.
item.dc:creator: Omar El Housni, Shuo Sun, Rajan Udwani

item.title: Online Coordinated Scheduling of EV Battery Charging and Heating in Cold Environments
item.description: arXiv:2602.11561v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Electric vehicle (EV) adoption in cold regions is hindered by degraded EV charging performance at low temperatures, which necessitates effective battery thermal management during charging. Given the coupling of battery charging and heating dynamics, this paper explores the benefits of online coordinated charging and heating control, rather than performing them separately. Specifically, we first build queue models for both battery charging and thermal dynamics. Then, we formulate an optimization problem to minimize the system cost of a charging station, which allows us to coordinate charging and heating through maintaining queue stability. To solve the problem, we develop an online coordinated charging and heating control algorithm using Lyapunov optimization techniques. The proposed algorithm is prediction-free and has provable feasibility and optimality guarantees. Numerical experiments based on real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our proposed method compared to existing benchmarks.
item.dc:creator: Xiaowei Wang, Yize Chen, Yue Chen

item.title: Non-Gaussian Uncertainty Estimation via Semi-nonparametric Density
item.description: arXiv:2604.09375v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Accurate and efficient representation of non-Gaussian state distributions is critical for estimation, control, and decision-making, especially when the system is highly nonlinear. This paper develops a mathematical framework for estimating non-Gaussian uncertainty via semi-nonparametric (SNP), or Gallant-Nychka, densities. SNP densities use squared probabilists' Hermite polynomials to guarantee nonnegative probability densities while representing non-Gaussian behavior. For uncertainty propagation, once fitted to propagated state samples, SNP densities enable direct analytical density and probability evaluations without needing to tune additional hyperparameters besides the polynomial order. To enable their application to nonlinear dynamical systems, we derive analytic marginal and cumulative distribution functions and develop a lossless convex formulation of the coefficient estimation problem along a given sign branch. The approach is demonstrated on the chaotic Lorenz system and compared against Gaussian mixture models and Edgeworth approximations. Results demonstrate that SNP densities can accurately represent non-Gaussian state distributions while enabling direct probability and quantile evaluation, making them a promising tool for density estimation and uncertainty quantification in nonlinear estimation and control.
item.dc:creator: Aaron R. Liao, Kenshiro Oguri, Michele D. Carpenter

item.title: Convergence of Singular Dynamics Driven by Mixed Logarithmic Heat Gradients
item.description: arXiv:2605.12231v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the terminal behavior of singular deterministic and stochastic dynamics driven by convex or extrapolative combinations of logarithmic heat gradients. These equations arise in exact-score guided diffusion sampling, including classifier-free guidance. The rescaled potentials converge to weighted sums of squared support distances, but extrapolative mixing can produce limiting directions that depend on probability masses and lie outside the Clarke subdifferential of the limiting potential. A componentwise chain rule gives dissipation for the limiting differential inclusion. Posterior relative entropy yields finite deterministic kinetic action in logarithmic time, while a conditional free-energy estimate bounds expected energy increments uniformly in the restart time. For compactly supported laws, these estimates give energy convergence and equilibrium localization, almost surely for each fixed stochastic initialization; extrapolation requires a lower small-ball mass bound on the reference law. For finite atomic measures, we prove that the equilibrium set is finite for arbitrary site configurations. Every deterministic trajectory therefore converges to an equilibrium, and stochastic convergence holds almost surely for each fixed initialization, including endpoints at projection interfaces. At empirical endpoints with a unique nearest atom in each active support, deterministic trajectories admit a square-root heat-time expansion with an exponentially small remainder. The exponent 1/2 is sharp when the leading coefficient is nonzero. These results provide a geometric and dynamical framework for understanding terminal convergence in guided diffusion models.
item.dc:creator: Kang Liu, Enrique Zuazua

item.title: Accelerating Min-Max Optimization via Power-Law Stepsizes
item.description: arXiv:2606.01764v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We revisit the convergence guarantees of the Extragradient (EG) method for unconstrained biaffine min-max optimization. It is known that EG with a fixed stepsize achieves a $\Theta(T^{-1/2})$ last-iterate convergence rate, which is slower than the optimal $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1})$ rate attainable by incorporating additional mechanisms such as anchoring. Motivated by recent advances showing that dynamic stepsizes alone can significantly accelerate gradient descent, we ask whether dynamic stepsizes can similarly accelerate the last-iterate convergence of EG. We present the first positive result in this direction. Specifically, we provide a deterministic dynamic stepsize schedule that accelerates the convergence rate of EG to $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2/3+\varepsilon})$ for any $\varepsilon > 0$. We also show that this rate is nearly tight when the extrapolation and update steps of EG use the same stepsize. We then show that allowing different stepsizes for the extrapolation and update steps further improves the convergence rate to the near-optimal $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1+\varepsilon})$. Our analysis reduces stepsize scheduling to an optimization problem, whose solution leads to a stepsize schedule that follows (a discretization of) a power-law distribution. Our proposed stepsize schedules and analysis extend to other methods, such as Optimistic Gradient (OG), and suggest broader applicability to general min-max optimization problems.
item.dc:creator: Yue Wu, Weiqiang Zheng, Yang Cai, Haipeng Luo

item.title: Finite difference methods for a continuous-time heterogeneous agent model with recursive utility
item.description: arXiv:2606.23408v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose, analyze and test computational methods for solving a continuous-time heterogenous agent model with Epstein-Zin utility. Such recursive utilities allow the model to disentangle between risk aversion and intertemporal substitution. Having discretized the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equation arising in the model, we propose a Howard-Newton algorithm for the late resolution preference case, and a Howard-Tarski-Kantorovich algorithm for the early resolution preference case. We prove the convergence of the iterative algorithms. We obtain as a consequence the existence of solutions to the discretized HJB equations. In the late resolution case, we supply a priori estimates between the unique solutions of the continuous and discretized HJB equations.
item.dc:creator: Yves Achdou, Qing Tang

item.title: Heilbronn's Problem in the Unit Triangle: Computational Optimality Certificates for $n \le 8$
item.description: arXiv:2607.15021v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study Heilbronn's triangle problem in the unit right triangle, where $n$ points are placed to maximize the smallest of the $\binom{n}{3}$ triangle areas they span. We prove a boundary-structure result: unless all three vertices are occupied, some optimal configuration with $n \ge 5$ has at least four points on the boundary, one edge containing two of them. With the affine $S_3$ symmetry this fixes four boundary points and $n$ orientation variables in a mixed-integer model that certifies global optimality for all $n \le 8$ up to a relative gap of $10^{-4}$. For $n \le 7$ this independently confirms the known exact optima, the case $n = 7$ having been proved by Zeng and Chen with symbolic computation. For $n = 8$, where only bounds were known, it narrows the gap to Cantrell's configuration fourfold in 39 minutes on one machine. The optimum there is conjectured to be the real root of a septic obtained by Chen, Zeng and Zhou, which our reconstruction confirms to 250 digits. We show its Galois group is $S_7$, so on that conjecture no expression in radicals exists.
item.dc:creator: Nathan Sudermann-Merx

item.title: Integrating Learning and Optimization for Open Transport Capacity Pooling under Disruption
item.description: arXiv:2609.40296v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Disruptions can leave logistics networks short of capacity, yet outside capacity is hard to use: incumbent models are private, provider records are incomplete, and offers stay hidden until a costly request for quotation (RFQ). We introduce open capacity pooling as a budgeted provider-discovery problem that links which capacity need to pursue, whom to contact, and which verified offer to admit. The alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) coordinates incumbents without sharing models, and the resulting capacity gaps direct discovery. A machine-learning layer fitted before search ranks providers by predicted capability and a fleet-size proxy from directory records and large language model (LLM) readings of self-descriptions. Verification reveals offers, reduced-cost screening admits them, and re-optimization updates the gaps and prices. Under fixed offers and exact coordination, a full-revelation reference reaches the finite-universe optimum, while budgeted discovery remains heuristic. We evaluate the mechanism on 4,509 real firms in three US regions excluded from predictor training, using scenarios calibrated to seven historical disruptions and simulated availability, offered quantities, and prices. With 80 RFQs, about 1% of exhaustive search, the mechanism recovers 19-43% of the full-information value of outside transport, against 2-6% for random search, and saves USD 73,000-104,000 per event before search and contracting costs. At tight RFQ budgets, gap-guided need selection and learned ranking are complements in these testbeds. LLM reading helps rank capabilities that records omit, such as refrigerated service, but its operating value varies by region. The results support combining record-based learning with coordination-derived gaps under limited search budgets.
item.dc:creator: Yujia Xu, Walid Klibi, Benoit Montreuil

item.title: The Big Match under translation-invariant charges
item.description: arXiv:2610.19646v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study finite two-player zero-sum stochastic games in which the stream of expected stage payoffs is evaluated by a translation-invariant charge on the set of stages. Every patient valuation, that is, every diffuse charge that obeys the time value of money principle, is translation-invariant. By Mertens and Neyman (1981), every finite two-player zero-sum stochastic game has a value; in particular, each player has, for every $\varepsilon>0$, a strategy that is $\varepsilon$-optimal for all patient valuations simultaneously. We show that this robustness breaks down for translation-invariant charges, even when the charge is fixed in advance. In the Big Match with $0$--$1$ payoffs, for every charge, Player~2 can guarantee that Player~1's payoff is at most $1/2$, but cannot guarantee any smaller bound. Nevertheless, we construct a fixed translation-invariant charge such that, for every strategy of Player~1 and every $\delta>0$, Player~2 has a pure reply yielding payoff less than $\delta$. Consequently, the Big Match has no value under this charge. More generally, the supremum of the payoffs that Player~1 can guarantee ranges over $[0,1/2]$ as the translation-invariant charge varies. This contrasts with finite Markov decision processes, where every stationary Blackwell optimal strategy is optimal for every translation-invariant charge.
item.dc:creator: Abraham Neyman

item.title: Event-Triggered Funnel Control for Output Reference Tracking of Unknown Nonlinear Systems
item.description: arXiv:2610.22153v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We propose an event-triggered zero-order hold implementation of the funnel controller for output reference tracking of unknown nonlinear systems. The control input is updated only when the deviation between the current and the last transmitted input exceeds a prescribed threshold, reducing the number of input updates while maintaining closed-loop performance guarantees by incorporating an auxiliary integral state to compensate for the error introduced by the zero-order-hold input. We establish a uniform lower bound on the inter-event intervals excluding Zeno behavior, and derive a growth condition on the nonlinear dynamics that ensures global existence of the solution for arbitrary, predefined sampling schedules. The theoretical results are illustrated by numerical simulations.
item.dc:creator: Janina Schaa, Thomas Berger

item.title: FOMTools: Development and AI-Assisted Code Generation for First-Order Methods
item.description: arXiv:2610.26743v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present FOMTools, an open-source Python package for developing, analyzing, and deploying first-order algorithms for parametric linear and convex quadratic optimization. The user specifies an iteration in Python, with syntax close to its mathematical description. The package represents the iteration as a computation graph of affine and piecewise affine operations. To analyze worst-case performance, FOMTools formulates a mixed-integer verification problem that maximizes a convergence residual over a specified set of problem instances and initial iterates. For probabilistic performance analysis, a batched GPU simulator collects algorithm trajectories and computes statistical bounds on the probability of exceeding a specified convergence tolerance. From the same algorithm description, FOMTools generates specialized solver code for embedded hardware, multicore CPUs, and GPUs. The package first generates the numerical data, factorizations, and matrix-vector routines without any agent. A coding agent then translates the iteration into C or CUDA code and iteratively optimizes the implementation. After each phase, the package runs the generated code on sampled inputs and compares it with a reference execution. FOMTools also serves as a CVXPYgen backend, generating and optimizing solvers for parametric CVXPY problems. We demonstrate FOMTools on sparse coding, network optimization, optimal control, and portfolio rebalancing. The verification bounds reveal worst-case behavior that sampling misses. The generated solvers run up to two orders of magnitude faster than NumPy implementations, and they outperform hand-written GPU code and the OSQP solvers generated by CVXPYgen.
item.dc:creator: Vinit Ranjan, Daniel Deza, Anushka Acharya, Jisun Park, Bartolomeo Stellato

item.title: Transport-Free Lower Bounds for Ollivier--Ricci Curvature in Higher-Order Networks: Scope, Tightness, and Computational Applications
item.description: arXiv:2405.13302v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study how the Bauer--Jost--Liu curvature bound applies to hypergraph Ollivier--Ricci curvature (ORC) and how its accuracy depends on local mass and geometry. An explicit weighted-graph representation shows how the graph theorem applies. A transport construction transfers the bounds to monotone pairwise hyperedge aggregations. We analyze endpoint cancellation under laziness, quantify the exact improvement over the earlier mixture bound, and characterize the extremal geometry at fixed endpoint and overlap statistics. Further results quantify worst-case slack, stability, and exactness on isolated hyperedges. A capacity-constrained short-detour refinement uses additional geometric information and improves monotonically as the query budget increases. As a computational application, a threshold cascade preserves exact transport decisions. Numerical verification and public-hypergraph experiments examine tightness, walk dependence, and aggregation, including evaluations on 42,940 finite pairwise comparisons and 64,620 public-data instances. Together, the results specify the scope, equality mechanisms, and computational uses of BJL-type hypergraph bounds.
item.dc:creator: Wonwoo Kang, Heehyun Park

item.title: Accelerated Approximate Optimization of Multi-Commodity Flows on Directed Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2503.24373v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We provide $m^{1+o(1)}k\epsilon^{-1}$-time algorithms for computing multiplicative $(1 - \epsilon)$-approximate solutions to multi-commodity flow problems with $k$-commodities on $m$-edge directed graphs, including concurrent multi-commodity flow and maximum multi-commodity flow. To obtain our results, we provide new optimization tools of potential independent interest. First, we provide an improved optimization method for solving $\ell_{q, p}$-regression problems to high accuracy. This method makes $\tilde{O}_{q, p}(k)$ queries to a high accuracy convex minimization oracle for an individual block, where $\tilde{O}_{q, p}(\cdot)$ hides factors depending only on $q$, $p$, or $\mathrm{poly}(\log m)$, improving upon the $\tilde{O}_{q, p}(k^2)$ bound of [Chen-Ye, ICALP 2024]. As a result, we obtain the first almost-linear time algorithm that solves $\ell_{q, p}$ flows on directed graphs to high accuracy. Second, we present optimization tools to reduce approximately solving composite $\ell_{1, \infty}$-regression problems to solving $m^{o(1)}\epsilon^{-1}$ instances of composite $\ell_{q, p}$-regression problem. The method builds upon recent advances in solving box-simplex games [Jambulapati-Tian, NeurIPS 2023] and the area convex regularizer introduced in [Sherman, STOC 2017] to obtain faster rates for constrained versions of the problem. Carefully combining these techniques yields our directed multi-commodity flow algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Li Chen, Andrei Graur, Aaron Sidford

item.title: Branch-and-Cut for Mixed-Integer Nash Equilibrium Problems
item.description: arXiv:2506.02520v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We consider mixed-integer Nash equilibrium problems in which each player solves a mixed-integer optimization problem parameterized in the rivals' strategies. We distinguish standard Nash equilibrium problems (NEPs), where the parameterization acts only on the cost functions, and generalized NEPs (GNEPs), where the strategy spaces may also depend on the rivals' strategies. We introduce a branch-and-cut (B&C) algorithm for such games that, upon termination, either computes a pure Nash equilibrium or decides that none exists. The main idea is a bilevel reformulation based on the Nikaido--Isoda function. Using bilevel-optimization techniques, we obtain a tractable relaxation of this reformulation and embed it into a B&C framework. Depending on the setting, we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of suitable cuts and finite termination. For GNEPs, we adapt intersection cuts (ICs) from bilevel and mixed-integer linear optimization. Such cuts exist under assumptions that hold, e.g., for pure-integer GNEPs with decoupled concave objectives and linear coupling constraints. Since ICs may become arbitrarily shallow, we complement them with a fallback strategy that fixes recurring integer profiles and ensures finite termination in a relevant setting. For NEPs, suitable cuts always exist via best-response inequalities, and our method terminates finitely whenever the set of best-response sets is finite. This holds, e.g., if (i) the cost functions are concave in the players' own continuous strategies and the strategy sets are polyhedral, or (ii) the cost functions only depend on the player's own strategy and the rivals' integer strategy components. Numerical results on various NEPs and GNEPs show that our tailored B&C method outperforms directly applying the state-of-the-art bilevel solver MibS on the tested integer and generalized knapsack instances.
item.dc:creator: Alo\"is Duguet, Tobias Harks, Martin Schmidt, Julian Schwarz

item.title: A Learning Stability Profile for Finite-Dimensional Learning Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2512.21208v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a finite-dimensional sensitivity framework for studying stability in learning systems whose states include representations, parameters, and update variables. The central object is the \emph{Learning Stability Profile}, a collection of directional sensitivity operators that records how perturbations in inputs, parameter initialization, and update mechanisms propagate along a specified learning trajectory. The main result is a Lyapunov criterion for controlling this profile. Under explicit regularity, coercivity, and dissipation assumptions, an incremental Lyapunov energy yields uniform or exponentially decaying bounds on the associated linearized transition operators. The result is stated as a sufficient stability criterion, not as an unconditional converse theorem. The framework also distinguishes terminal decay, profile-wise boundedness, and subexponential growth, avoiding the identification of nonpositive growth exponents with uniform boundedness. The profile is then specialized to several standard learning mechanisms. Spectral bounds give forward sensitivity estimates for feedforward networks. Dissipativity and step-size restrictions give stability bounds for residual architectures. Mean-square contraction assumptions yield parameter and update sensitivity bounds for stochastic gradient methods. Locally Lipschitz systems, including piecewise-linear networks, proximal maps, projected updates, and recurrent or state-space recursions, are handled through Clarke generalized Jacobians and variational Lyapunov inequalities. The resulting framework provides a common stability language for architecture, optimization, stochasticity, and nonsmoothness. Its role is structural: it organizes known stability mechanisms within one perturbation calculus while keeping the hypotheses needed for each guarantee explicit.
item.dc:creator: Ronald Katende

item.title: Sample-wise Constrained Learning via a Sequential Penalty Approach with Applications in Image Processing
item.description: arXiv:2601.16812v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In many learning tasks, certain requirements on the processing of individual data samples can arguably be formalized, in an intelligible way, as strict constraints of the underlying optimization problem, rather than by means of arbitrary penalties that often require heavy trial-and-error tuning. In this paper we show that, in these scenarios, learning can be carried out exploiting a sequential penalty method that allows to explicitly deal with constraints. For the proposed algorithm we show that, under classical assumptions and in the considered learning scenario, penalty subproblems can provably be solved in finite time with suitable guarantees of approximate stationarity in expectation; we also show that, when the latter condition is guaranteed for the subproblems, the overall sequential scheme possesses almost sure convergence properties to KKT-stationary points of (general) constrained problems. The results of experiments on sandbox and real-world image processing tasks show that the method is indeed viable to be used in practical deep learning scenarios.
item.dc:creator: Francesca Lanzillotta, Chiara Albisani, Davide Pucci, Daniele Baracchi, Alessandro Piva, Matteo Lapucci

item.title: A Unified Matrix-Spectral Framework for Stability and Interpretability in Deep Learning
item.description: arXiv:2602.01136v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop a unified matrix-spectral framework for analyzing stability and interpretability in deep neural networks. Representing networks as data-dependent products of linear operators reveals spectral quantities governing sensitivity to input perturbations, label noise, and training dynamics. We introduce a Global Matrix Stability Index that aggregates spectral information from Jacobians, parameter gradients, Neural Tangent Kernel operators, and loss Hessians into a single stability scale controlling forward sensitivity, attribution robustness, and optimization conditioning. We further show that spectral entropy refines classical operator-norm bounds by capturing typical, rather than purely worst-case, sensitivity. These quantities yield computable diagnostics and stability-oriented regularization principles. Synthetic experiments and controlled studies on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 confirm that modest spectral regularization substantially improves attribution stability even when global spectral summaries change little. The results establish a precise connection between spectral concentration and analytic stability, providing practical guidance for robustness-aware model design and training.
item.dc:creator: Ronald Katende

item.title: A Function-Space Stability Boundary for Generalization in Interpolating Learning Systems
item.description: arXiv:2602.03514v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern learning systems often interpolate training data while still generalizing well, yet it remains unclear when algorithmic stability explains this behavior. We model training as a function-space trajectory and measure sensitivity to single-sample perturbations along this trajectory. We propose a contractive propagation condition and a stability certificate obtained by unrolling the resulting recursion. A small certificate implies stability-based generalization, while we also prove that there exist interpolating regimes with small risk where such contractive sensitivity cannot hold, showing that stability is not a universal explanation. Experiments confirm that certificate growth predicts generalization differences across optimizers, step sizes, and dataset perturbations. The framework therefore identifies regimes where stability explains generalization and where alternative mechanisms must account for success.
item.dc:creator: Ronald Katende

item.title: Multiscale Supervised Unbalanced Optimal Transport Flow Matching
item.description: arXiv:2605.16529v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Unbalanced optimal transport (UOT) provides a principled framework for modeling single-cell transitions and birth-death dynamics, but its high computational cost limits scalability to large-scale datasets. Although single-cell data often contain hierarchical annotations and known transition priors, existing UOT approximations rarely exploit this multiscale structure or prior knowledge. We introduce Multiscale Supervised Unbalanced Optimal Transport Flow Matching (MUST-FM), a simulation-free framework that scales UOT by leveraging hierarchical data structure. MUST-FM further supports an optional supervised formulation that incorporates transition priors, such as cell lineages, to guide the learning of displacement fields and mass variations. Experiments show that MUST-FM reduces computational overhead while achieving robust and biologically meaningful trajectory inference, enabling dynamic modeling of atlas-scale single-cell datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/QiangweiPeng/MUST-FM.
item.dc:creator: Qiangwei Peng, Lezhi Chen, Peijie Zhou

item.title: No-Harm Physics-Informed Inverse Learning with Residual-Calibrated Uncertainty
item.description: arXiv:2606.07153v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Physics-informed learning is increasingly used for partial differential equation (PDE)-governed inverse problems, but its reliability remains difficult to certify. This paper develops a no-harm certification-and-selection framework for physics-informed inverse learning. A learned reconstruction is accepted only when its residual-calibrated radius is no worse than the baseline radius, namely when $$R_{\mathrm{learn}}\le R_{\mathrm{base}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{safe}};$$otherwise, the method returns the baseline. The certificate combines data, physics, boundary or initial-condition, and optimization residuals. Under a conditional stability estimate, these residuals yield an a posteriori reconstruction-error bound and a deterministic uncertainty radius. A high-probability certificate is also derived for physics residuals estimated from independent random collocation points. Numerical tests on Poisson source recovery, inverse heat reconstruction, limited-angle tomography, elliptic coefficient identification, and stochastic residual validation show that the selector accepts certified improvements, rejects shifted, hallucinated, or unfinished candidates, and becomes conservative in strongly ill-posed regimes. The framework is therefore a certification-and-selection layer, not another reconstruction architecture.
item.dc:creator: Ronald Katende

item.title: A Twin gradient method for unconstrained optimization
item.description: arXiv:2607.11575v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We propose a new strategy for gradient-based unconstrained optimization, involving two parallel sequences of iterates that cooperate to determine their stepsizes via a \textit{Twin-Step} principle. Rather than minimizing the objective function individually, the algorithm selects steplengths that minimize the Euclidean distance between the two gradient based processes occurring simultaneously at each iteration. The theoretical analysis shows that the convergence of the mutual distance is governed by the angle between the search directions. In particular the effectiveness of the overall process degrades as the directions approach parallelism. To ensure robustness against collinearity, we introduce a hybrid framework, Twin-ABB$_{\min}$, which switches to the Adaptive Barzilai--Borwein method when the geometric cooperation becomes ineffective. Extensive and very promising numerical results evidence that the Twin phase creates favorable initial conditions for subsequent BB-type iterations.
item.dc:creator: Anna De Magistris, Michiel E. Hochstenbach, Gerardo Toraldo

item.title: On the Column Number of Delta-Modular Matrices: an $O(m^2 \Delta)$ Bound via the Shifted Heller Constant
item.description: arXiv:2608.06215v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we build on the analysis initiated by Averkov and Schymura (2022) and prove that the shifted Heller constant for matrices with $m$ rows is at most $m^2 + m$ for all sufficiently large $m$. Consequently, the number of distinct columns of a $\Delta$-modular matrix $A \in Z^{m \times n}$ of rank $m$ is at most $O(m^2 \Delta)$. This improves upon the earlier bounds of $O(m^4 \Delta)$ and $O(m^2 \Delta^2)$.

item.title: A Nearly Quadratic Lower Bound for Linear Optimization over Convex Bodies in the Membership Oracle Model
item.description: arXiv:2609.30215v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove nearly quadratic lower bounds for randomized algorithms for linear optimization and uniform sampling over convex bodies in the membership oracle model. For linear optimization, this matches the known nearly quadratic upper bound up to a polylog factor in the dimension. For uniform sampling, this improves on the previous linear lower bound. Our construction also implies the same lower bound for volume estimation.
item.dc:creator: Santosh S. Vempala

item.title: Simple Strategy-Iteration with Dantzig's Rule is not Strongly Polynomial on Turn-Based Deterministic Games
item.description: arXiv:2610.27386v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study turn-based deterministic zero-sum games with discounted and long-run average costs. For discounted costs, we establish exponential and superpolynomial iteration lower bounds for the simple strategy-iteration method with Dantzig's rule under unrestricted costs and unit weights, respectively. To the best of our knowledge, we establish for the first time that the method is not strongly polynomial, and this remains true even when all action costs belong to $\{-1,0,1\}$. For long-run average costs, we extend the Dantzig counterpart in~\cite{zhongye2026} to the two-player setting and prove that it terminates at an optimal strategy profile. However, a similar counterexample construction establishes an exponential iteration lower bound for termination with unrestricted costs. This construction does not extend to unit weights, for which we prove that the algorithm admits a strongly polynomial implementation.

item.title: Dispersive Tree Agreements for Multi-Robot Coordination
item.description: arXiv:2610.31540v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-robot coordination of nonlinear systems is naturally formulated as joint-space optimal control subject to joint constraints. Existing methods that approach joint optimality remain largely centralized and offline, while decentralized, real-time counterparts target safe navigation without pursuing the joint optimum. This paper develops a decentralized, real-time planner that approaches the joint optimum as an anytime process. We extend a recent single-robot framework that searches dispersive trees of forward-propagated commands to coordinate a multi-robot team near-optimally. We first show that the inter-robot coupling can be effectively replaced by some local constraints, under which locally grown dispersive trees contain a near-optimal agreement. It is this structure that the robots pursue by a negotiation driven by decentralized column generation. In the quiescent limit, this negotiation is shown to settle on a near-optimal agreement. Our real-time protocol, WarpWeaver, runs the negotiation asynchronously over a receding horizon and closes on quiesced agreements even when deadlines cut it short. In simulation, WarpWeaver reduces total travel time by up to 22% against centralized offline planners on the Dynobench suite and by up to 16% against a decentralized real-time baseline, and outperforms a task-specific planner on networked navigation. Hardware experiments on six robots planning onboard demonstrate real-world implementability.
item.dc:creator: Shashank A. Deshpande, Blake T. Edwards, Jonathan P. How

item.title: Readiness-Constrained Pre-Islanding Dispatch for Military Microgrids
item.description: arXiv:2610.40078v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Military installation energy readiness depends on having sufficient resources to sustain mission-critical loads throughout a prolonged utility outage. This paper develops a method to help operators manage energy resources during normal grid-connected operation while preserving islanded readiness. A robust viability kernel identifies combinations of battery energy, fuel, and load-shifting capability sufficient to sustain critical load under uncertain demand and photovoltaic generation. A probability bound translates stochastic generator start failures and recovery into a deterministic generator count selected to meet a specified availability requirement at islanding. Case studies for a fourteen-day islanding requirement at 0.999 islanding-entry availability show that advance warning of an outage can be used to prepare resources to meet a higher readiness requirement before islanding begins. The case studies further demonstrate that economic-only operation and the evaluated fixed battery reserve policy can fail to sustain critical load for the required duration, whereas enforcing the resource-dependent requirement preserves readiness at a modest increase in modeled grid-connected operating cost. These results demonstrate how active resource management can preserve long-duration energy readiness. The framework also helps commanders understand how readiness changes with operating conditions, even when the available resources remain the same.
item.dc:creator: Aidan Looney, Annie Weathers, Nicholas Judson
